blocks.text: Practice long questions for the whole of Chapter 13 (Thermoregulation and Osmoregulation), in the shape of a Board long question: each theory question carries 4 marks (describe, explain, compare, label and describe a structure, give examples), as one 4-mark part or in 1+3 / 2+2 sub-parts. Each question has a full model answer.

blocks.prompt: 1 Homeostasis keeps the internal environment stable. (i) Define homeostasis and name its important processes. (ii) Explain how the control centre and effectors keep the internal environment at its set points, with an example. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
(i) (1 mark) Homeostasis is the vital process by which living organisms maintain a stable internal environment despite changes in the external environment. Its important processes are thermoregulation, osmoregulation and excretion.

(ii) (3 marks)
Control centre: it receives information from the receptors, processes it and sends appropriate messages to the effectors. These messages keep the internal environment within a narrow range of set points, which are optimal for the body's function. The brain, spinal cord and endocrine glands act as control centres.
Effectors: the parts of the body that respond to the control centre's message. Muscles respond by contracting and glands by releasing their secretion; in this way they restore the internal environment to its set points.
Example: when body temperature drops below the set point, effectors in the skin and muscles cause shivering and vasoconstriction. This increases heat production and raises the body temperature back to the set point.

book_ref.quote: These messages ensure that the internal environment remains within a narrow range of set points

blocks.prompt: 2 Define a negative feedback system. Explain how it regulates body temperature when it rises above 37°C. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Negative feedback: a mechanism in which the output or product of a system reduces the activity of the system. It is the most common form of regulation; examples are the regulation of body temperature, blood glucose levels and hormone secretion.

Regulation of body temperature:
1. Body temperature exceeds the set point of 37°C.
2. Thermoreceptors in the hypothalamus of the brain detect this change.
3. They send signals to the control centre, the thermoregulator in the hypothalamus.
4. The control centre sends messages to effectors, e.g. sweat glands.
5. The effectors produce sweat, which lowers the temperature.
6. The output (temperature lowered to the set point) influences the thermoreceptors negatively, so they stop sending messages to the control centre and the response stops.

book_ref.quote: The output of this process (lowering of temperature to the set point) influences the thermoreceptors negatively

blocks.prompt: 3 Positive feedback works in the opposite direction to negative feedback. (i) Explain the positive feedback loop of childbirth. (ii) How can unregulated positive feedback cause health problems? (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
(i) (3 marks) In positive feedback, the output increases the activity of the system and enhances the original stimulus. It is less common than negative feedback and occurs in processes needing rapid and significant changes, e.g. blood clotting, labour and childbirth.
Childbirth:
1. Contractions of the uterus send nerve impulses to the control centre (part of the hypothalamus).
2. The control centre signals the pituitary gland to release oxytocin.
3. Oxytocin stimulates further contractions of the uterus.
4. These send more nerve impulses to the hypothalamus, leading to release of more oxytocin.
5. The loop continues until the baby is born.

(ii) (1 mark) In severe inflammation or infection, immune cells release proteins called cytokines, which further stimulate the immune response. If this positive feedback is not properly regulated, it can lead to excessive inflammation and tissue damage.

book_ref.quote: Oxytocin then stimulates further contractions of the uterus

blocks.prompt: 4 Osmoregulation and osmoconformers. (i) Define osmoregulation and state why it is essential. (ii) Explain why osmoconformers are found mainly in marine water, giving examples. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
(i) (2 marks) Osmoregulation is the maintenance of the balance of water and solutes in the body fluids. It ensures that the body fluids do not become too dilute or too concentrated. It is essential for many physiological processes, including maintaining proper blood pressure, enabling the proper function of organs and regulating metabolism.

(ii) (2 marks) Osmoconformers allow the osmotic concentrations of their body fluids to match their environment. They cannot maintain the concentration of water and solutes in their bodies, so these change with the surrounding medium and they remain isotonic to it. Such animals can survive only where solute concentrations are relatively stable, such as marine water. Examples: all marine invertebrates, some freshwater invertebrates, and some marine vertebrates like hag fishes, sharks and rays.

book_ref.quote: Osmoconformers are the animals which allow the osmotic concentrations of their body fluids to match their environment

blocks.prompt: 5 Compare the osmotic problems of freshwater animals and hypotonic marine animals, and the methods each uses to solve them. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Freshwater animals are generally hypertonic to the surrounding water, while hypotonic marine animals live in water with a much higher salt concentration than their tissues. Their problems are therefore opposite, and so are their solutions:

book_ref.quote: To compensate for the water loss, marine animals drink seawater continuously

blocks.prompt: 6 Terrestrial animals constantly lose water. Describe their anatomical, physiological and behavioural adaptations for maintaining osmotic balance. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
The problem: terrestrial animals lose water by evaporation from respiratory surfaces, through the skin and with excretion of waste. Water intake (drinking and food) plus metabolic water must equal the water lost.

Anatomical adaptations: relatively impermeable outer layers prevent evaporative water loss:
• insects: waxy exoskeleton made of chitin;
• reptiles: waterproof scales made of keratin;
• mammals and birds: dead, keratinized skin cells and oil-secreting glands in the skin.

Physiological adaptations: the kidneys play a vital role in retaining water. Ammonia, the primary waste of protein metabolism, is converted into urea or uric acid, which need less water for excretion. Some animals, like the Kangaroo Rat, survive entirely on metabolic water produced in cellular respiration.

Behavioural adaptations: many desert animals stay underground in the heat of the day and come out only at night, when the air is cooler and more humid. They feed on seeds of desert plants with large stores of carbohydrate.

Anhydrobiosis: certain invertebrates like tardigrades become dormant after losing almost all body water and revive years later when water returns.

book_ref.quote: These animals have anatomical, physiological, and behavioral adaptations to maintain osmotic balance

blocks.explanation: In many animals osmoregulation is coupled with removal of nitrogenous wastes, which are excreted as water solutes; animals of different habitats excrete different forms:

blocks.prompt: 8 Nitrogenous wastes are changed on land. (i) Why do terrestrial animals convert ammonia into urea or uric acid instead of excreting it directly? (ii) Explain the formation of uric acid in humans and how its excess causes gout. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
(i) (2 marks) Ammonia is highly toxic and one gram needs 500 mL of water to dissolve it to a nontoxic level; only freshwater animals can afford this. Terrestrial animals must conserve water, so they convert ammonia in the liver into urea (less toxic, 50 mL of water per gram) and excrete it through the kidneys. Insects, desert animals, birds and most reptiles face an extreme water challenge in arid habitats and cannot afford even urea; they spend a lot of energy to make uric acid, which is even less toxic, less soluble, forms precipitates and needs just 1 mL of water per gram.

(ii) (2 marks) Humans also excrete a small amount of uric acid in urine. It is a by-product of the breakdown of purines, which are found in many foods, particularly meat and some vegetables, and it is produced in the liver. In healthy people most uric acid is excreted in urine. When there is an excess of uric acid in the blood, uric acid crystals form in joints and tissues, causing the painful condition gout.

book_ref.quote: Humans also excrete a small amount of uric acid in urine

blocks.prompt: 9 Explain how ectotherms regulate their body temperature by behaviour, and why their low metabolic rate makes this necessary. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Ectotherms: animals that gain most of their body heat from external sources; their internal temperature generally fluctuates with the surroundings. Most invertebrates, and among vertebrates fishes, amphibians and reptiles, are ectotherms.

Why behaviour is needed: in ectotherms the metabolic rate is very low. They cannot produce enough heat to raise and maintain their body temperature, so they rely on heat from the environment.

Behavioural thermoregulation:
• Too cold: they bask in the sun (gaining heat by radiation) or sit on a warm rock (gaining heat by conduction).
• Too hot: they seek shade or burrow into the cool earth.
• In very cold climates, they become dormant during the coldest months.

book_ref.quote: If they are too hot, they seek shade or burrow into the cool earth

blocks.prompt: 10 A lizard is called both an ectotherm and a poikilotherm, while a bird is both an endotherm and a homeotherm. (i) Explain the basis of each pair of terms. (ii) State one advantage of being a poikilotherm. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
(i) (3 marks) Animals are classified in two ways:
• On the basis of heat source: ectotherms gain most body heat from external sources (fishes, amphibians, reptiles such as the lizard); endotherms generate most body heat through internal metabolism (birds and mammals).
• On the basis of ability of thermoregulation: poikilotherms cannot maintain body temperature within narrow limits, and it usually matches the environment (all invertebrates, and fishes, amphibians and reptiles); homeotherms maintain relatively constant internal temperatures regardless of environmental fluctuations, using 'thermostats' (hypothalamus in the brain) (mammals and birds).
So the lizard, which takes heat from outside and lets its temperature follow the environment, is an ectotherm and a poikilotherm; the bird, which makes its own heat and keeps its temperature constant, is an endotherm and a homeotherm.

(ii) (1 mark) Poikilotherms do not need to consume massive amounts of food to 'fuel' a constant temperature, so they can survive in nutrient-poor environments where a homeotherm would starve.

book_ref.quote: Their body temperature varies considerably, usually matching the temperature of environment

blocks.prompt: 11 Describe how endotherms produce and retain body heat, and how homeotherms keep their body temperature constant. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Endotherms:
• They generate the majority of their body heat through internal metabolism.
• They maintain a relatively constant body temperature, often higher than the environment.
• When it gets cold, they may shiver (muscle contractions) or burn brown adipose tissue for heat.
• Most have insulation to retain heat, such as hair, feathers or fat.
• Examples: birds and mammals.

Homeotherms:
• They maintain relatively constant internal body temperatures regardless of environmental fluctuations.
• They use 'thermostats', the hypothalamus in the brain, to trigger cooling or heating responses.
• Examples: mammals and birds; humans keep their internal temperature at roughly 37°C in very cold or very hot environments.
• Humans are endothermic homeotherms and regulate temperature by negative feedback: skin thermoreceptors signal the hypothalamus (which also has thermoreceptors), and it signals muscles and glands to make corrective responses.

book_ref.quote: These animals maintain relatively constant internal body temperatures, regardless of environmental fluctuations

blocks.prompt: 12 Compare the responses of the human body to cooling (hypothermia) and to overheating (hyperthermia), stating how each response works. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: In both cases the hypothalamus, informed by thermoreceptors, sends signals to muscles and glands; the responses are opposite. The thermoreceptors also stimulate the higher brain centres, so we feel warmth or coldness and can take actions such as bathing or turning fans or heaters on.

book_ref.quote: When body temperature rises above 37°C (hyperthermia), vasodilation occurs

rows: Vasoconstriction: less blood flows to the skin, so less heat is lost from blood
Vasodilation: the arterioles supplying the skin capillaries widen, so more blood flows just beneath the epidermis and more heat is lost
Shivering (spasmodic contraction of skeletal muscles) produces heat
Sweating: evaporation of sweat carries heat away and cools the body
Goosebumps: tiny muscles at hair follicles contract; air trapped in erected hair insulates
Metabolic rate increases, producing heat
Thyroid may decrease thyroxine, lowering basal metabolic rate and internal heat production
